final_message:
All three programs print the correct output for every sample (`s1`, `s2`, `s3`). 300 random small graphs also gave identical output from all three. Those covered repeated sources, self-loops, unreachable nodes and graphs with no edges. I removed my scratch files, so the folder holds only the three deliverables plus the SPEC.md and samples.

**Algorithm.** It is single-source shortest paths, run once per source. Each run gives the reachable count, the distance sum, the maximum distance, and the smallest node at that maximum. All three build a compact adjacency structure (CSR) and skip self-loops. Repeated sources reuse the earlier answer.

**`rust/src/main.rs`**
- It hand-parses the input bytes and builds the adjacency arrays with a counting sort. Each edge is stored as a (neighbour, weight) pair, so one lookup gets both.
- Shortest paths use Dial's bucket queue: a circular array of weight-sized buckets, with no heap. That is possible because weights are small integers. If a weight ever reached 65536 or more, it falls back to a binary heap on packed keys.
- `Cargo.toml` release profile: LTO, `codegen-units=1`, `panic=abort`.
- On my generated 300k-node, 900k-edge grid-like graph with 6 sources, it ran in about 0.2 to 0.25 s.

**`plain.py`**
- It runs Dijkstra with `heapq`. Each heap entry is one packed integer (`dist<<shift | node`), which is faster than tuples.
- Adjacency is a list of packed integers per node.
- It writes bytes to stdout, so Windows doesn't turn `\n` into `\r\n` and break the exact match with the `.out` files.
- On my large test graphs it took about 11 s on the earlier, smaller-distance graph (it was not re-timed on later ones).

**`fast.py`**
- A NumPy parser reads all the integers from the file bytes in one pass.
- It builds the adjacency by packing each directed edge into one int64 and sorting once. This replaced an `argsort` that cost about 0.9 s.
- Shortest paths use a vectorised, delta-stepping style search (buckets of distance width `maxw//2`). Each round takes the nodes inside the current distance window, gathers all their edges at once, and applies the improvements with `np.minimum.at`. Repeated entries are dropped without sorting.
- The final statistics are computed with NumPy.
- On my large test graphs it took about 1.1 to 1.7 s, though timings were noisy because other programs were running on the machine.

I tested on grid graphs I generated myself, shaped like `s3`. I did not have a real benchmark-size input.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
